hook_text: Block a syringe of air and you can push it halfway in. Block a syringe of water and it will not budge. The reason is ten diameters wide.
clip_script: Gas particles are far apart, ten diameters between them, mostly empty space. Push and the space closes up: it squashes, and it springs back. Liquid particles touch. Push and there is nothing to close; you would have to crush the particles themselves. It will not budge. So compressed air is a spring: it stores energy, which is why a burst air hose whips and a tyre can explode. It lags, so you cannot position an air cylinder exactly. It cushions, which is why air in brake lines gives a spongy pedal and a late stop, and why mechanics bleed brakes. Liquid moves instantly and holds solid. Brakes, jacks, excavators: liquid. Air tools, bus doors, dentist's chairs, tyres: air. Trucks use both.
visual_style: Whiteboard particle boxes, sparse dots versus packed dots, with a piston squashing one and stalling on the other; a brake pedal with a bubble in the line; two columns of machines.
mood: Clear science, everyday examples, a note of respect for stored energy.
pacing: Particles, the two syringes, three effects, the two columns.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find three pneumatic and three hydraulic machines on your street.
